entries.title: Conspiracy theories can provide answers, but not peace
entries.summary: Twenty-five years after 9/11, conspiracy theories about the terrorist attacks persist. But even as an attempt to make sense of a tragedy, psychologists say the benefit in conspiracy ideation or belief is short-lived.
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

Conspiracy theories can provide answers, but not peace

September 9, 2026

Twenty-five years after 9/11, conspiracy theories about the terrorist attacks persist. But even as an attempt to make sense of a tragedy, psychologists say the benefit in conspiracy ideation or belief is short-lived.

Psychology is not an exact science. That may irk a few researchers in the field. But it is important to mention upfront: Researching the psychology of conspiracy theories — why people are drawn to believing them and the effect they have on those people — is a complicated field of research, and conclusions are difficult to derive.

That is due, in part, to one of the basic problems with psychology, whether it's in treatment or in research, and that is that it relies on people's self-awareness.

If we take the example of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, some people continue to maintain it was "inside job", orchestrated by a secretive and powerful club of evil doers in the US government, intent on controlling citizens' lives by fear. And that may be true. But it may also be true that you, as a believer in such a theory, have always felt powerful people — your parents or teachers — have controlled and curtailed your agency in life. You may even have a false memory of how the terrorist attacks evolved on that day in 2001. Then, if someone asked you, "What really happened?", could you really say it for sure? I couldn't.

Self-report data is an issue in conspiracy research

Whether as patients or participants in a study, we may be asked to "self-report" — to look inside ourselves and express how we feel and why.

Self-reporting is an established way of measuring conspiracies, said Neil Dagnall, a professor of psychology at Manchester Metropolitan University, in an interview with DW.

But self-report data are "not perfect," he added.

They can be difficult data to handle because each judgment a person makes about themselves is relative, inherently subjective, and open to outside influence and bias. People's answers can change from day-to-day, especially when they involve emotions or feelings about mental state, depending on a multitude of events and experiences in our lives. In addition, there is no common scale.

Say, for example, you and a friend were asked, "Are you happy?" You may both say "yes," but your reasons for doing so may be completely different and be subject to different variables. The same goes for a question like, "Do you believe in conspiracy theories?"



"The judgment I'm making is a relative one. What's my norm? Am I comparing it to my friends who don't believe in conspiracies or am I in a group of people who do believe in conspiracies? We're always making relative judgments about our psychological propensities," said Dagnall. 

Which suggests we're unlikely to ever get a definitive answer. Self-report data suggest correlations, not causation.

In a study on conspiratorial beliefs and well-­being, which Dagnall co-authored and published in May 2026, "self-report data" was specifically highlighted as a limitation.

This makes it very difficult to assess whether "conspiracy belief" or "conspiracy ideation" is good or bad for people and their sense of well-being. Especially as people who seek and believe in conspiracy theories often start out with a skewed view of reality.

Observing behavior can offer clues

There are ways of "triangulating" self-­report data, as the authors of the study put it, to get a more reliable, objective reading of a person's emotional, or psychological, state.

For example, psychologists use behavioral observations, like measuring heart rate variability, or Galvanic Skin Responses such as the electrical conductance of a person's skin, which is affected by sweating under stress. You can also retest participants' self-reported data, and therefore its reliability, by asking the same questions at different points in time.

But there is another factor that complicates research into the psychology of conspiracy theories, and that is that they, and people who believe in them, are more common than we like to think or admit (even when we believe them ourselves).

"The idea that people who believe in conspiracies in general populations are remarkable or different is not true," said Dagnall.

The truth: 'conspiracies theories are common'

Most of us, at some point in our lives, are bound to see something strange or stressful in society and question whether we, as individuals or as a member of a group, accept the accepted truth of how that thing or event came about. It can be a healthy sign of a questioning mind.

There are positive examples of conspiracy theories that happened to kickstart investigations that then revealed the horrible truth of government corruption.

Take Partygate during the COVID pandemic in the UK or — the mother of all conspiracies — Watergate during the Nixon Administration in the US.

And there are other conspiracy theories, such as the one that nobody has ever landed on the moon, which you can either take seriously or laugh about.

It all comes down to "the degree to which we engage in conspiracies generally, and the extent to which they interfere and disrupt our everyday lives," said Dagnall.

For Dagnall, who doesn't believe in the 1969 moon landing, it doesn't seem to disrupt his daily life — at least, that is what he self-reported to DW.

But for some people, conspiracy theories are disruptive and can lead to a sustained sense of dissatisfaction.

"Ample studies suggest that exposure to conspiracy theories or belief in them might lead to more negative emotions, heightened anxiety, or even paranoid thoughts," said Zuzanna Molenda, a researcher at the Polish Academy of Sciences and lead-author of a 2023 study on emotion dysregulation and belief in conspiracy theories.

Some people may be primed to more readily believe in conspiracy theories because they generally struggle to deal with psychological threat and distress. When they then seek answers in conspiracy theories, their pre-existing negative psychology may be enhanced.

"If anything, the available evidence suggests that rather than help people manage difficult emotions, conspiracy beliefs may be accompanied by or contribute to further distress," wrote Molenda in an email to DW.

No long-term benefit from conspiracy belief

There may be some psychological benefit to conspiracy theories, said Molenda, but only in the short term.

"Conspiracy beliefs can provide people with a sense of explanation and understanding when events feel uncertain or difficult to make sense of. For some people, they might also be a source of entertainment and fun. For others, they can provide a sense of belonging and connection with others who share the same beliefs, and they can be an important part of social identity," Molenda said.

But these potential benefits do not necessarily translate into better well-being in the longer term, said Molenda.

In the end, we're all searching for meaning and purpose in life. If we find a satisfactory answer, it gives us, what psychologists call presense — a direction in life, and that is good.

But if your search only leads to more uncertainty, more anxiety, and more doubt in your purpose in life, then that's bad. "And people who believe in conspiracies are asking questions but not getting answers," said Dagnall.

Edited by: Kristie Pladson

entries.title: UK rules out cyberattack after major flight disruptions
entries.summary: Airports across the UK continue to face delays and cancellations after a flight processing system failure. The UK's transport secretary has summoned the CEO of National Air Traffic Services (NATS) for an explanation.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

UK rules out cyberattack after major flight disruptions

September 9, 2026

Airports across the UK continue to face delays and cancellations after a flight processing system failure. The UK's transport secretary has summoned the CEO of National Air Traffic Services (NATS) for an explanation.

Martin Rolfe, CEO of the UK's National Air Traffic Services (NATS), has ruled out a cyberattack after a major interruption Tuesday in operations at British airports. 

"We will be doing a very, very thorough and full investigation," Rolfe told the BBC on Wednesday morning.

More than 1,000 flights were cancelled and delayed due to air traffic control problems that started Tuesday morning and lasted for several hours. NATS said a problem involved an issue with the flight processing system.

Although NATS said the problem was resolved, more than 150 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, and more delays were expected throughout the day.

London's Heathrow Airport on Wednesday said "some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew," and advised travelers to check flight status before heading to the airport.

"There are going to be dozens of cancellations in the morning of flights coming into Heathrow because, basically, the flights didn't go out tonight," travel journalist Simon Calder said to Sky News. "The consequences will be horrible," he added.

Questions over the UK's network

The UK's Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said Wednesday that she had summoned Rolfe for a closer explanation of what caused the malfunction, amid concerns over the UK's air traffic network.

This is not the first time a major system failure has affected British airports. In August 2023, several flights were cancelled due to a "system meltdown," costing airlines $135 million. In 2025, problems with flight radars affected several airports in the UK, including  Heathrow Airport.

"I am seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the ‌job," Alexander said on X.

Ryanair,  Europe's biggest airline, said at least 150,000 passengers using its services experienced delays of up to eight hours. Two hundred of its flights were cancelled. 

For the second time, the airline demanded that NATS CEO Rolfe resign.

Rolfe told Sky News he accepted "full responsibility" but did not say if he was considering stepping down.

NATS provides air control traffic services to 15 UK airports. It is a public-private partnership which is partially owned by airlines including British Airways and easyJet, pension funds and the government.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: The billion-euro trade driving Europe's eels to extinction
entries.summary: Traffickers are making big bucks smuggling millions of critically endangered eels across continents, using suitcases on planes and legal loopholes to deliver them to dinnerplates. Where are the smuggling hotspots?
entries.content:
September 9, 2026

Traffickers are making big bucks smuggling millions of critically endangered eels across continents, using suitcases on planes and legal loopholes to deliver them to dinnerplates. Where are the smuggling hotspots?

In Plentzia, a small waterfront town close to bustling Bilbao, eel fishing has long been part of daily life. Now fisherfolk across Spain's Basque Country can no longer catch the animals, a prized delicacy at the center of what authorities describe as one of the world's most lucrative wildlife trafficking trades.  

The regional ban is meant to protect the European eel, a critically endangered species, which has seen population declines of around 95% since the 1980s. Yet local fishermen argue the regulations punish those who adhere to them, while criminal networks profit from a billion-euro trade in  illegally caught eels.  

"So it's the Basque fishermen who will make the eel extinct when the rest are allowed to fish?" said Unai Eizaguirre who's been fishing eels for 30 years and is now facing the prospect of income shorfalls. "It's ridiculous."

Conservationists support the ban as an emergency response in the face of multiple threats from pollution and climate change. But marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says longer-term measures, like removing hydroelectric dams that block migration routes and kill eels with their turbines are also needed.  

"I don't know if the eel has time to wait for these projects to show their effects," said Diaz, who works with local marine research institute AZTI.

Eel smuggling as lucrative as drugs

Part of what makes European eels so vulnerable is their remarkable life cycle, which was, until relatively recently, a source of mystery. Scientists now know adult eels migrate thousands of kilometers from European rivers to the Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic, their only known spawning grounds. They breed and then die, leaving their larvae to drift to Europe. By the time they reach rivers, they've transformed into tiny, transparent "glass eels."

Today, only about 12% survive the journey from the Sargasso to the Gulf of Biscay and connected waterways, Diaz told DW. The young glass eels conservationists are trying to protect are the most valuable in the illegal trade, fetching up to €9,000 ($10,400) per kilogram.

"You can compare it with drug trafficking. Every year they seize tons of illegally caught eel in Europe," said Eizaguirre. "The big business lies in trafficking them to Asia," adding that the huge profits and comparatively small fines for smaller infractions by local fishers make the risk worth it. However, when criminal organizations are involved, penalties can be substantial with fines up to 6 times the value of illegally smuggled eel.

Demand in countries such as China, South Korea and Japan is driving prices. As is a biological peculiarity: So far, it's been exceedingly difficult to get eels to reproduce in captivity. This means fish farms — where the eels are raised before being sold to premium restaurants — need a steady stream of young from the wild. Sometimes, the same smuggled eels come back to Europe as fillets for the sushi market. 

Conservationists had hoped pressure on the species would ease when the EU banned export of the species outside the bloc in 2010. Instead, organized crime groups have increasingly muscled in on the market, with the illegal trade now generating an estimated €3 billion in profits in peak years.

"Our estimated maximum was always 100 tons of glass eels smuggled annually. That's already around 300 million fish," said Florian Stein, head of policy and science at the German Angling Association. But information from his contacts in the illegal trade have led him to the conclusion that it was a "very conservative estimate."

International law enforcement agencies are also cracking down, with Europol's Operation Lake seizing 22 tons of glass eels and arresting 26 suspects between 2024 and 2025.

"There has been a lot of pressure from law enforcement throughout Europe," said Interpol's Sanchez Romero. "That's why the criminal groups always look for new routes."

Eels smuggled in suitcases along complex routes

Stein, who wrote his doctoral dissertation on international eel smuggling and advises the German government, said trafficking has increased since 2020, and illegal trade routes have become more complex.

"Ten years ago, Madrid airport was still one of the biggest smuggling hotspots," he added. This was due to its proximity to fishing grounds in northern Spain and Portugal.

Increased checks by Spanish authorities on flights to East Asia forced traffickers to adapt. Experts now say a new route running through North Africa via Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal has become increasingly important.

Geography is one reason the route is attractive. The Strait of Gibraltar is 14 kilometers at its narrowest point and a busy maritime junction. "We know that many drugs are also transported through this strait," Moroccan investigative journalist Yassir Al-Makhtoum told DW.

European eels also inhabit rivers and estuaries in Morocco. Though the country has banned the export of glass eels smaller than 12 centimeters (4.7 inches), it is building a legal domestic eel trading industry. Experts fear that's acting as a cover for trafficked animals coming in from Europe.

From Morocco, smugglers then move eels along numerous routes to Asia. The means are not always sophisticated. Glass eels can be transported in ordinary suitcases on domestic flights. They're placed in bags filled with a little water and insulated to keep their temperature stable. They can survive for up to 48 hours in those conditions. Once in Asia, they go to the fish farms.

A species running out of time

Eels are an important indicator species for the health of ocean and riverine ecosystems because their long migrations across multiple habitats make them vulnerable to problems that could also harm other species. They also serve as important prey for herons, otters and larger fish.  

"But the impact of its disappearance is difficult to predict," said marine biologist Diaz.

Under EU regulations, member states must undertake measures to allow 40% of adult eels to return to the Sargasso Sea to spawn. Diaz also wants to ensure at least 40% of glass eels make it back from the Sargasso Sea.

But European eels are not the only eel species under threat. A proposal to protect all freshwater eel species from illegal and unsustainable trade was rejected at the 2025 CITES wildlife conference. For Stein such protection is key.

"The proposal should be on the table again at the next conference. I just don't know how else we can get a handle on this problem," said Stein, adding more lobbying and coalition building is needed to advocate for a ban.

“The eel for us is more than just a fish,” said Unai Eizaguirre. “It's been part of our identity for centuries.” For fishermen like him, better protection for the eel represents a chance at a sustainable future.

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

The research for this story was sponsored by: The Med Mosaic.

entries.title: India: 5 baby orangutans rescued, smuggling suspected
entries.summary: Five young orangutans, not native to India, were found in an Odisha forest, sparking suspicion of an international smuggling operation. Meanwhile, India said it was not involved in the BAPS-Eiffel Tower row.
entries.content:
India

India: 5 baby orangutans rescued, smuggling suspected

Published September 9, 2026last updated September 9, 2026

Five young orangutans, not native to India, were found in an Odisha forest, sparking suspicion of an international smuggling operation. Meanwhile, India said it was not involved in the BAPS-Eiffel Tower row.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Forest officials have rescued five baby orangutans thousands of kilometers from their native habitat
  • Indian officials say they have nothing to do with the BAPS-Eiffel Tower controversy
  • Preparation for the BRICS summit is in full swing, but staying at a luxury hotel could burn a serious hole in your pocket

Below is a roundup of the top headlines from India from Wednesday, September 9.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Delhi faces luxury hotel crunch ahead of BRICS summit

Delhi faces luxury hotel crunch ahead of BRICS summit

As New Delhi prepares to host world leaders for the 18th BRICS summit set for this weekend, the Indian capital's luxury hotel sector is experiencing a shortage of space along with price increases, according to local media reports. 

A check of booking platforms found no availability at the Taj Mahal and The Oberoi for September 11-12, while the Taj Palace had no rooms for September 10-12 and The Leela Palace wasn't accepting bookings for the same dates, according to local media.

At the ITC Maurya, where rooms were available, starting nightly rates exceeded Rs 230,000 ($2400/€2100), news agency PTI reported.

K B Kachru, president of the Hotel Association of India, said the summit is exposing gaps in India's hospitality capacity.

"The BRICS Summit alone will put considerable focus on room inventory and that spotlight is exposing a hard truth: our hospitality infrastructure has not kept pace with our tourism ambition," he said.

He told PTI that India has only about 200,000-220,000 branded hotel rooms nationwide.

The summit is also compressing demand across a wider window as delegates arrive early and extend stays, potentially forcing other travelers to pay a premium, look farther from central Delhi, or shift travel dates.

Skip next section India distances itself from Eiffel Tower row over Hindu group's visit

India distances itself from Eiffel Tower row over Hindu group's visit

India's Ministry of External Affairs on Tuesday distanced itself from the controversy arising from Hindu group Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha's (BAPS) visit to the Eiffel Tower.

BAPS had earlier apologized after the Eiffel Tower closed Monday when staff went on strike over allegations that female workers were sidelined during a visit by roughly 100 members of the organization. 

"As to the particular issue pertaining to the Tower, this is a matter purely between the entities concerned," MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said during a press briefing, confirming India was aware of the controversy following BAPS's inauguration of France's first traditional Hindu temple near Paris on Sunday.

Jaiswal also addressed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's virtual address at the temple's opening, calling it standard practice for the government to convey "good wishes" on such occasions and saying there was "no cause for any comment" on the matter, local media reported.

BAPS said the visit had been pre-coordinated with the tower's operators and that, to its knowledge, no one was denied access, though it apologized to anyone "hurt or inconvenienced."

Tower operator SETE acknowledged accepting a request to limit "interactions with women," calling it a mistake it should not have agreed to.

Eiffel Tower staff, in their own statement, condemned what they called instructions that left female employees "sidelined, replaced, and rendered invisible based on their gender," saying some were told to leave their posts or avoid certain areas while the delegation was present.

Read more about the controversy here. 

Skip next section Baby orangutans rescued, sparking international smuggling probe

Baby orangutans rescued, sparking international smuggling probe

Indian forest officials rescued five baby orangutans in the eastern state of Odisha on Tuesday, with authorities suspecting the great apes were smuggled into the country from Southeast Asia.

The animals, not native to India, were found in a forest in the Balasore district. Local legislator Goutam Buddha Das told The Telegraph newspaper that villagers first spotted the orangutans dangling from a tree and initially mistook them for monkeys, before alerting forest officials that their appearance didn't match. 

He said the area's coastal location suggested the animals could have arrived by sea from Indonesia.

"I demand a high-level inquiry to find out who is involved in the racket," Das said.

Balasore forest officer Pratik Prakash Indalkar said the three male and two female orangutans were examined by veterinarians, found to be in good health, and given food and oral rehydration solution before being transferred to Nandan Kanan Zoo in Bhubaneswar for quarantine.

Odisha Environment Minister Ram Singh Khuntia said the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau is now investigating how the animals reached India. 

"We suspect that an international racket might be involved in this," he told the IANS news agency. Authorities are also examining whether the animals were destined for sale to buyers in Kolkata.

Orangutans are native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra. Only about 104,000 remain in the wild, according to the World Wildlife Fund, down from more than 230,000 a century ago.

The Tapanuli orangutan is critically endangered, with fewer than 800 animals thought to be left.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, once again bringing you the latest from across India. 

When forest officials in India's Odisha state found five baby orangutans on a patrol, thousands of kilometers from their natural habitat, the officials suspected they were trafficked into the country from Southeast Asia.

In other news, the Indian government has steered clear of controversy in the row over Hindu group BAPS's visit to the Eiffel Tower.

Finally, New Delhi is gearing up to host the 18th BRICS Summit from September 11 to 13. With security protocols being heightened and hotel prices skyrocketing, the non-high-profile Delhi visitors may be in for a hit to their pockets.

For this and more, follow our live blog.

entries.title: Trafficked into fraud: An African crisis situation in Cambodia
entries.summary: Cambodia's crackdown on scam operators is stranding young African trafficking victims in the Asian country with no money, no passport and no prospects.
entries.content:
September 9, 2026

Cambodia's crackdown on scam operators is stranding young African trafficking victims in the Asian country with no money, no passport and no prospects.

Southeast Asia has long emerged as a major hub of highly organized online fraud operations, targeting people all around the world.

According to the United Nations, these operations generate tens of billions of dollars annually, having long surpassed the illegal drug trade as the most profitable activity for criminal networks, as reported by the United States Institute of Peace.

However, those who fall prey to scams and other fraudulent activities aren't the only victims of these criminal rings; alone in Southeast Asia, the scam industry is powered by at least 300,000 trafficked workers from 66 countries. They are routinely subjected to torture, sexual abuse and forced labor, according to a recent UN Human Rights report.

African nationals now form the largest group of those trafficked to and stranded in countries like Myanmar and Cambodia, without any viable pathway to go back home, says the NGO Freedom Collaborative.

In Cambodia, one of the main obstacles to helping stranded Africans return home is that many countries on the continent, such as Uganda, Liberia, Ghana and Nigeria, lack consular representation.

But there are other reasons.

"Some countries have zero interest," says Montse Ferrer, co-regional director of Amnesty International, who also blames the home countries for their inaction.

"They're not even picking up the phone, let alone providing the paperwork or the money for them to go back."

Cambodia's reluctant crackdown on scam operators

Ferrer believes that the Cambodian government also has an interest in keeping scam trafficking victims in the country. This is because many of the victims now have overstay fines for their visas against their names in Cambodia, reaching thousands of dollars in many instances.

"They don't allow NGOs to provide the support these people need, and instead they have resorted to arresting and threatening them," Ferrer told DW.

Following great pressure from the international community — including threats of financial sanctions by the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and the European Union — Cambodia did eventually agree to launch a crackdown on the scamming industry earlier this year.

According to the Cambodian Ministry of Information, the initiative resulted in many arrests and triggered a mass exodus of dubious operatives from scamming industry.

But the crackdown also created a secondary crisis: Thousands of trafficked foreign workers remain stranded in the country without documentation nor legal status; now, they also lack shelter and money in many instances, NGOs say.

Many who have sought help in Cambodia have reportedly been placed in immigration detention, while others have to sleep rough and beg for food.

Instead of being given protection, trafficking victims often face stigmatization and abuse on the street of the capital Phnom Penh and elsewhere.

Lured to Cambodia under false pretenses

Emmanuel David is one of those stuck in Cambodia. The 28-year-old Liberian national arrived there in 2025 after a treacherous irregular journey originating in Vietnam.

"My friend told me there was work in Cambodia, but he did not explain that it was scamming work," David explained.

The scamming company had offered him a lucrative deal of making around $800 (€700) per month, which is more than double the average wage for qualified individuals in Liberia.

The reality hit quite differently: Once there, David was forced to work 14 hours a day to deceive women on various dating apps to part with their money.

But David was initially unable — and later unwilling — to meet the set target quota of scams per day.

In response, the criminal group he worked for started billing him for food and accommodation through his wages and later even confiscated his belongings, including his passport.

David says he also faced substantial physical violence, including beatings, for four months.

Eventually, he left "with no documents and no money," and is now hoping to find a way back to Liberia.

His story is far from unique.

'Hundreds' of Africans trafficked to criminal compounds

Another survivor, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation, also recounted how he was "beaten and [subjected to] electric shocks."

The abuse resulted in him having to be hospitalized for three weeks, and he is now unable to pay his medical bills.

Pia Oberoi, chief of the Right to Development Section at UN Human Rights, told DW that "despite the promise of a good salary, most come out in debt."

She also confirmed that a growing number of trafficking victims in Southeast Asia come from African countries, "because there is clearly a recruitment industry that's built around Africa, targeting African nationals."

Other victims have corroborated this development, describing hundreds of Africans packed into heavily fortified compounds.

"Once you're inside there's no way out," an informant, who also chose to remain anonymous, told DW.

He said the compounds have their own laws, and that sexual abuse and psychological violence are an integral part of how they operate.

The police, he says, just turn a blind eye.

No government assistance from any direction

Amnesty International speaks of an unfolding humanitarian crisis, warning that escapees are widely being treated as criminals rather than as trafficking victims, a sentiment the UN shares.

"They shouldn't be punished for crimes they were forced to commit," the UN's Oberoi highlights.

Several of the victims contacted by DW meanwhile said their governments were notably "slow" to help with their repatriation.

DW also attempted to contact several African foreign ministries for comment but has yet to receive a response.

A statement issued by the Cambodian government meanwhile said that more than 700 compounds run chiefly by Chinese nationals had been raided, with 58,266 foreign nationals deported and nearly 30,000 suspects arrested over the past year.

However, the Cambodian government did not reply to DW's direct request for further information.

The UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM) explained it's trying its utmost to help the trafficking victims; but in the face of severe budgetary constraints, it can only provide "limited, prioritized support."

Fear, guilt and stigma

Humanitarian groups also warn of a high risk of victims being re-trafficked. This is a danger even for those who have somehow managed to return to their countries of origin.

In some instances, those who come back home are stigmatized as a failure — "a situation that is really unbearable," says Ferrer.

Emmanuel David is a prime example: He feels obliged to to apologize to his family for not returning a success.

When asked about his little daughter, he simply says "Daddy can't go home without money."

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: Ukraine, Russia trade drone strikes, killing 6
entries.summary: At least four people were killed, and 29 others were injured, in a Ukrainian attack on a Russian Black Sea port. Meanwhile, Russian drones struck a crossing on the Ukraine-Moldova border, killing two.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine, Russia trade drone strikes, killing 6

September 9, 2026

At least four people were killed, and 29 others were injured, in a Ukrainian attack on a Russian Black Sea port. Meanwhile, Russian drones struck a crossing on the Ukraine-Moldova border, killing two.

A Ukrainian drone attack on the Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk overnight killed at least four people, including a child, Russian officials said Wednesday.

Veniamin Kondratyev, the governor of the Krasnodar region in southern Russia, said 29 others were injured in the drone attack.

Ukraine has frequently targeted Novorossiysk, a port city that is a major outlet for Russian oil and grain exports.

Earlier on Wednesday, the mayor of the city, Andrei Kravchenko, had said the debris from a Ukrainian drone fell onto several businesses and nearly landed on a residential building, sparking fires.

In the nearby town of Anapa, falling drone debris damaged three homes and a kindergarten, Kondratyev said, adding that there were no casualties.

Russia's Defense Ministry said nearly 600 Ukrainian drones had been shot down overnight.

Two civilians killed in Russian attack on border crossing

Russian drone strikes overnight on a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, meanwhile, killed at least two civilians, the regional governor Oleh Kiper said on social media.

Three people were wounded in the strike on the Starokozace border crossing, around 500 kilometres (310 miles) south of Kyiv, Ukraine's State Border Guard Service said.

The strikes forced the checkpoint to close temporarily, Kiper said, adding that multiple fires broke out as a result of the attack.

Ukrainian emergency officials also said the capital, Kyiv was attacked overnight. While some fires were started, there were no casualties.

What is the latest in US-brokered peace talks?

Russia on Tuesday resumed its near-daily airstrikes on Kyiv after a brief pause while US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow for talks.

At least five people were killed in Kyiv on Tuesday, officials said.

Russia also said President Vladimir Putin had had an "extremely frank" phone call with his US counterpart Donald Trump on Tuesday, as Washington continues to press Ukrainian and Russian officials to hold face-to-face talks to end the war.

Ukraine has suggested talks that could take place in September, but Russian officials have said it is "too early" to discuss specifics such as a venue or dates for the talks.

Despite US pressure, talks between Moscow and Kyiv have yielded no results beyond sporadic prisoner swaps.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Merz, Weidel face off after AfD state win

Published September 9, 2026last updated September 9, 2026

Alice Weidel and Friedrich Merz are facing off in the Bundestag days after the AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt has put new pressure on the German chancellor. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) leader Alice Weidel and Chancellor Friedrich Merz are facing each other in parliament
  • The general debate comes days after the AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt's state election
  • The result has increased pressure on Merz, who is being blamed by some in his conservative Christian Democratic Union for the party's poor performance

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, September 9, 2026:

Skip next section Germany weighs risks to national intelligence amid far-right gains

Germany weighs risks to national intelligence amid far-right gains

German federal and state officials are discussing how to guard against potential security risks posed by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) following its election victory in Saxony-Anhalt.

Security officials are particularly concerned about how sensitive intelligence could be protected if the AfD were to lead a state government, including the risk that information could be passed to Russia.

The heads of Germany's federal domestic intelligence agency and its 16 state counterparts are expected to discuss the AfD during a regular meeting in Stuttgart.

Security sources rejected reports that the three-day meeting had been specially convened because of the Saxony-Anhalt election. However, officials are expected to consider ways of preventing sensitive information from being improperly disclosed.

The AfD won 43.8% of the vote in Sunday's election, narrowly missing an absolute majority.

Officials do not intend to cut a possible AfD-led government off from intelligence entirely, the Reuters news agency reported, citing security sources.

Information would still need to be shared, for example, if authorities received warnings of a planned attack in Saxony-Anhalt or if the state obtained intelligence about threats elsewhere.

However, officials could restrict the sharing of some information on right-wing extremists because the AfD itself has been classified as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization in several German states.

There are also concerns that intelligence services in allied countries could become more reluctant to share sensitive information with Germany if AfD officials had access to it.

North Rhine-Westphalia state Premier Hendrik Wüst, of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), called for a joint federal-state working group involving domestic intelligence officials, constitutional law experts and other specialists to examine how authorities should deal with the AfD.

Wüst cautioned against rushing into an attempt to ban the party, saying any review should remain open-ended and consider other possible legal measures.

Banning a political party should be the last resort for protecting the constitution, he said.

Skip next section AfD demands its candidate lead Saxony-Anhalt under any coalition deal

AfD demands its candidate lead Saxony-Anhalt under any coalition deal

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt says it would only cooperate with other parties if its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund is elected state premier in the first round of voting.

The stance puts particular focus on the left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), whose support could give the AfD the seats it needsafter the far-right party fell just short of an absolute majority in Sunday's state election.

"That is the condition for cooperation, regardless of which party it is, and therefore of course also with the BSW," deputy AfD state leader Hans-Thomas Tillschneider told The Pioneer news platform.

The AfD emerged as the strongest party in Sunday's state election with 43.8% of the vote but fell short of an absolute majority.

The BSW won just over 5% of the vote and entered the state parliament.

BSW representatives have said they are prepared to hold talks with all parties, including the AfD, but have so far ruled out a formal coalition.

A few days before the vote, Wagenknecht spoke on TV broadcaster ntv about overlapping policy preferences of BSW and AfD voters: "These are people who have similar concerns: They want controlled migration, they do not want this uncontrolled migration and they want above all that politics is again conducted in their interests, that their lives are the focus."

Tillschneider also said cooperation with the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) could be possible if the party abandoned its "firewall" against working with the AfD.

Under the firewall, other German political parties have pledged not to cooperate with the far right AfD.

"A CDU that gives up its firewall against the AfD and opens itself up to cooperation could be a partner," he said.

He argued, however, that the CDU was currently moving in the opposite direction.

Skip next section Attempted Leipzig airport drone attack planned in Russia, Merz says

Attempted Leipzig airport drone attack planned in Russia, Merz says

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Wednesday that an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport had been prepared in Russia over a period of months and that a major disaster had only narrowly been avoided.

"This attack was planned in Russia for months and was specifically targeted at Germany, and only by pure chance was major material damage and harm to people prevented," Merz told the Bundestag.

The alleged attack has become part of a broader debate in Germany over Russian hybrid threats and the country's ability to protect critical infrastructure.

Merz made the remarks days after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won the Saxony-Anhalt state election. The party has repeatedly called for closer relations with Moscow.

Russia has denied involvement in the Leipzig incident. Its foreign minister has described Germany's accusations as "the start of a real war."

Skip next section Merz blasts AfD's 'remigration' policy

Merz blasts AfD's 'remigration' policy

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz sharply attacked the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) over its migration policy during Wednesday's Bundestag debate.

He described the party's concept of "remigration" as "nothing other than ethnic cleansing based on skin color and origin."

Merz said such a policy would also have severe consequences for Germany's labor market, where many people with migrant backgrounds are employed.

"If things were to happen the way the AfD wants, the skilled trades in Germany could no longer function, not a single care home would be able to operate, not a single hospital would be able to operate, and not a single restaurant could be run," Merz said.

"That would be the result of your remigration policy," he told AfD lawmakers.

Merz said there was agreement within his governing coalition that many people without a right to remain permanently in Germany should be deported.

"But we distinguish carefully between those who work in Germany, who contribute to our prosperity, who are welcome in Germany, and those who do not have a permanent right to remain and who must leave our country again," he said.

The government made that distinction carefully "in contrast" to the AfD, Merz added.

Skip next section Merz hits back at AfD after Saxony-Anhalt vote

Merz hits back at AfD after Saxony-Anhalt vote

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in the German parliament, the Bundestag, gave a barbed response to opening remarks from the far-right Alternative for Germany's (AfD) co-leader Alice Weider, who lambasted Germany's ruling coalition as a "failure." 

The Bundestag debate comes days after the AfD's after its strong showing in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, warning the party against assuming it was on course for broader majorities.

"Ms Weidel, today you can barely contain yourself," Merz told AfD co-leader Alice Weidel during the Bundestag's general debate on Wednesday. "But you do not have an absolute majority, and you will not achieve one in Germany."

"Nowhere in Germany will you win majorities with this politics," Merz said. "You are, and you remain a destructive force."

Merz acknowledged that the AfD had achieved "a remarkable election result in every respect" in Saxony-Anhalt.

"The voters spoke pretty clearly. They also sent us, and me personally, a clear message," he said.

However, he stressed that the AfD had failed to achieve its stated goal of securing an absolute majority in the state parliament in Magdeburg.

Merz accused the AfD of showing "contempt for our democratic institutions" and of repeatedly denigrating representatives of the state.

"You are and will remain a destructive force," Merz said.

He said there was a "deep divide" between the AfD and the other parties in foreign, European, social and peace policy.

Merz also accused the AfD of damaging German interests through its friendly stance towards Russia.

"The only thing that really threatens Russia and Putin is the appeal of democracy," he said. "And yet you are obviously still standing on Russia's side."

"You are part of the problem we have in Germany — and we will resist that with everything at our disposal."

Skip next section AfD's Weidel says Merz coalition is 'over' after state vote

AfD's Weidel says Merz coalition is 'over' after state vote

Alice Weidel, co-leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), said Chancellor Friedrich Merz's governing coalition had been rejected by voters after the AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt.

Speaking in the Bundestag's general debate in her first direct encounter with Merz since Sunday's state election, Weidel said voters wanted a change of political direction rather than "more of the same."

"The voters in Saxony-Anhalt have made it absolutely clear to you, in the language of democratic choice: black-red is over," Weidel said, referring to the traditional party colors of the conservative CDU/CSU and center-left Social Democrats within the governing coalition.

Weidel also attacked the government's fiscal policy, accusing Merz of pursuing unprecedented levels of borrowing.

She said Germany's public finances had been "shattered" and accused the chancellor of leaving behind "scorched earth."

"You are driving Germany towards national bankruptcy in record time," Weidel said.

She described the government's draft budget as a "declaration of surrender" by the coalition and claimed it was unconstitutional.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from DW's newsroom in Bonn.

The leaders of Germany's two biggest political rivals are facing off in the Bundestag for a general debate supposed to focus on the government's budget, but which has taken on added political significance days after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) beat the governing center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in Saxony-Anhalt.

entries.title: The Bayeux Tapestry in London: What's behind the hype?
entries.summary: The exhibition of the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum is eagerly anticipated across the UK, as the medieval masterpiece is considered by many to be a symbol of the country's identity.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

The Bayeux Tapestry in London: What's behind the hype?

September 9, 2026

The exhibition of the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum is eagerly anticipated across the UK, as the medieval masterpiece is considered by many to be a symbol of the country's identity.

First, let's start with a clarification: Strictly speaking, it's not actually a tapestry, since tapestries are woven, whereas this artwork is an embroidery on linen. Nevertheless, it is commonly referred to as such.

This pictorial narrative which is approximately 70 meters (230 feet) long, depicts the events surrounding the Norman Conquest of England in 1066, culminating in the Battle of Hastings and William the Conqueror's victory over Harold II.

The Norman Conquest radically changed England: Politics, laws and culture all came under the influence of Norman rule. The Bayeux Tapestry bears witness to this event; at the same time, it is an outstanding example of English craftsmanship from the Middle Ages and is seen by many Britons as one of the most important symbols of British identity, alongside the works of Shakespeare or Stonehenge.

The tapestry is thought to have been commissioned by the Bishop of Bayeux, William's half-brother, who was present at the battle, from embroiderers in southern England for the opening of his cathedral in 1070. Anglo-Saxon embroiderers were famous throughout Europe at the time for their skills. The work then made its way to France, where it remained for almost a thousand years — until now.

Why is the Bayeux Tapestry so important?

The Bayeux Tapestry is considered one of the most important pictorial monuments of the High Middle Ages. Many researchers view it as an elaborately crafted piece of propaganda that showed and explained William the Conqueror's victory to people at the time. Its scientifically disputed message is that Harold Godwinson, then Earl of Wessex, had sworn a sacred oath on relics to support William's claim to the English throne. He broke this oath when he had himself crowned king. The war is therefore portrayed as his just punishment. The fact that Harold had probably not taken the oath of his own free will is irrelevant to this woven narrative.

The embroidery is part of the UNESCO Memory of the World Register and, because of its 58 pictorial scenes, is sometimes referred to as "the world's oldest comic."

Accompanied by Latin inscriptions, the pictorial narrative depicts the horrors of war — including massacres, rolling heads and the death of a king.

But it is also a valuable historical document for researchers. The tapestry illustrates shipbuilding and military equipment in surprising detail, as well as everyday medieval life. Even Halley's Comet is shown in it — the comet was visible in the sky in 1066 and was interpreted by the Anglo-Saxons as a bad omen in the pictorial narrative.

Why did it take so long to get the tapestry on loan?

The tapestry is owned by the French state and had been placed on deposit with the City of Bayeux for display at the Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux.

Britain had already tried to borrow the tapestry for the coronation of Elizabeth II in 1953, as well as for various historical occasions afterwards, but France had always refused. The artefact was considered too fragile and the journey too risky. Finally, President Emmanuel Macron gave the green light last year for an exhibition at the British Museum — overriding the concerns of his experts.

Last September, the tapestry was taken down, packaged and initially placed in storage in a highly elaborate, six-hour procedure.

On July 9, it finally arrived in London in a secret transport operation, enclosed in a high-tech container that shielded it from all vibrations while maintaining a constant temperature and humidity level.

The British government has also insured the artwork for £800 million (around €932 million or $1 billion).

Where can you get tickets?

The British Museum has divided ticket sales into three phases. The first, covering September to December, began on July 1. All tickets sold out quickly, with up to 80,000 people reportedly trying to secure a slot at the same time. Many had to wait up to nine hours.

For those who missed out, there will soon be another chance — tickets for January to March will go on sale on October 21, and tickets for April to July in January.

The exhibition is being marketed as a "once-in-a-generation" event, and an extensive educational program is intended to involve schools across the country.

The British Museum is optimistic that the Bayeux Tapestry will help it set a new visitor record. The most popular exhibition in the museum's history to date is the 1972 "The Treasures of Tutankhamun," which attracted almost 1.7 million visitors.

No ticket? Here's an alternative

If you're now eager to see the tapestry but unsure if you'll land a ticket, you can also head to the town of Reading, around two hours west of London. There, you can see a faithful replica of the tapestry, which is itself already 140 years old.

Even back then, there was a strong desire in England to have this artwork in the country. In 1885, 35 embroiderers set to work for around a year. Using colored photographs as a reference, they reproduced the tapestry on a one-to-one scale. However, they did change one detail: Some figures on the original border are naked and in suggestive poses. Apparently, this was considered too scandalous in Victorian England. One figure was retouched in the corresponding photograph — and the embroiderers copied the alteration. As a result, the figure is depicted wearing underwear.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: EU sports commissioner says FIFA is 'damaging to football'
entries.summary: Speaking to DW, EU Commissioner Glenn Micallef hit out at world football's governing body over its "poor governance."
entries.content:
September 9, 2026

Speaking to DW, EU Commissioner Glenn Micallef hit out at world football's governing body over its "poor governance."

The European Union's sports commissioner has criticized world football's governing body FIFA over its controversial and now-aborted plans to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Speaking to DW at his Brussels office, Commissioner Glenn Micallef labeled the plans "another episode in a series of poor governance decisions that excessively commercialize the sport," adding, "It's damaging to football."

However, Micallef stopped short of calling on FIFA President Gianni Infantino to resign, amid growing pressure on him to step down. Asked whether FIFA was fit for purpose under Infantino, the commissioner insisted it wasn't for him to decide.

"That's a decision that belongs to national associations and federations," Micallef said. "I hope that they will have the chance to have an open process where they can discuss these things, where they can ensure accountability and responsibility for these issues."

Infantino faces ethics complaint

Micallef's comments come as the human rights group FairSquare submitted an updated complaint against Infantino to FIFA's ethics committee, joined by more than 100,000 signatures as part of its "Reboot FIFA" campaign.

The complaint details eight instances, four of them new, in which Infantino allegedly broke FIFA's ethics rules. These include the World Cup privatization plans and the reversal of US player Folarin Balogun's red card ban. All of the instances are linked to Infantino's relationship with US President Donald Trump.

In the complaint, seen by DW, FairSquare stated: "At a minimum, [Infantino] abused his power, violated his duty of political neutrality and his duty of loyalty in his efforts to ingratiate himself with the US president. The evidence that he sought to gain personally from this pattern of behaviour adds to the seriousness of the allegations."

Nicholas McGeehan, director of FairSquare, told DW that European football's governing body UEFA — among Infantino's fiercest critics — should get behind the complaint.

"I think [the ethics committee] is a paper tiger, but it is a mechanism that could be usefully deployed," McGeehan said. "You have a mechanism within this organization that could be used to get this guy out. So why aren't you supporting these complaints?"

World Cup for sale

FIFA's plans to sell 20% of the World Cup's commercial rights to private investors caused widespread outrage when they became public in July. UEFA announced in August it was considering bringing a criminal complaint against Infantino.

"Football is not for sale," Micallef told DW. "Yes, football needs investment, but that investment does not mean that football has to sell itself. The FIFA leadership is there … to make sure that football grows and reaches more people, but not to profit from it. Football belongs to us, the fans."

Despite the controversy, Infantino has confirmed he will stand for a fourth term as FIFA president next March. The governing body, which didn't respond to DW's request for comment, has closed ranks around its leader, saying previously that there was a "concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its president."

With no sign of Infantino budging, McGeehan called on the EU to intervene, questioning the ability of sports organizations to regulate themselves.

"I think there are a lot of football supporters who are dreadfully concerned about the way the game is run, but think that there is no way to fix it," McGeehan said. "And of course, there's always a way to fix it, and the way to fix it is politics."

Is FIFA breaking EU competition law?

FIFA's role as both competition organizer and football's global regulator has long raised concerns about a conflict of interest.

It is already the subject of a complaint to the European Commission's competition watchdog over its control over the international match calendar. The complaint, filed by the umbrella group representing Europe's domestic football leagues, alleges FIFA abuses its role to favor its own competitions. On Tuesday, the complaint was widened to include the women's game.

Micallef, meanwhile, did not rule out further action.

"The fact that sport is autonomous does not absolve it of its responsibilities under the law," he said. "So I don't exclude competition policy. Competition policy is a tool in our war chest, but I would much rather prefer to address these issues through dialogue than through competition lawyers."

Pointing to the EU's role last year in opposing Spanish and Italian league matches being played outside Europe — proposals heavily criticized by fan groups — Micallef expressed hope for change.

"The football community should never be underestimated. When those who are passionate about football and institutions come together and send a strong message, then we are a power to be reckoned with," he said . "We deserve proper governance. That's not too much to ask."

Matt Pearson contributed reporting to this article.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

entries.title: BRICS leaders gather in India, but does the group have a clear purpose?
entries.summary: The 18th BRICS summit takes place in India this weekend. Unlike last year, the leaders of China and Russia are coming. But does the expanded group have a clear common mission and purpose?
entries.content:
September 9, 2026

The 18th BRICS summit takes place in India this weekend. Unlike last year, the leaders of China and Russia are coming. But does the expanded group have a clear common mission and purpose?

In preparation for hosting the 18th BRICS summit in Delhi this weekend, India came up with a slogan which tried to keep the group's brand intact without alienating its many new members.

"Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" matches the acronym for the body's five original members — Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — whilst also denoting goals which the new members — Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates — can get behind.

"It's an elegant way to reinterpret BRICS so that the acronym represents a joint mission rather than country names," Mihaela Papa, director of the BRICS Lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, told DW.

For Sushant Singh, lecturer in South Asian Studies at Yale University, the vague slogan reflects India's desire as hosts to keep BRICS as low-key and neutral as possible.

"India doesn't want to offend Russia or China, but the fact is that Indians are looking more towards the United States these days. The desire to build up BRICS is not there."

India takes host role

Yet host India's status as a rising global geopolitical power has added clout to this year's gathering when compared with last year's summit in Brazil.

At the Rio de Janeiro gathering, six of the bloc's 11 heads of state skipped the event, including major players like Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Putin is expected to attend, while Xi Jinping is widely expected but not yet formally confirmed by Beijing. 

"The participation of China's top leadership is crucial," says Papa.

She also thinks it would be a significant sign of the BRICS' strength as a "stabilizing force" if the leaders of regional rivals Iran and the UAE were shown to be able to work together.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will attend but UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is expected to send representatives. Saudi Arabia, another Iranian foe, is also expected to. The country's BRICS status remains somewhat ambiguous, although current official BRICS materials generally list it as a member.

For India, the summit is as significant for the bilateral meetings it brings as much as for the BRICS gathering itself. Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are due to meet on Friday while the summit will also present an opportunity for Xi and Modi to speak face-to-face amid continued strain in the China-India relationship.

However, that does not mean much of substance will emerge from the weekend.

"In terms of concrete outcomes and what is achievable, I think it's going to be very, very limited," says Singh.

Modi has spoken of BRICS as an important forum for the 'Global South' to present a common front on various issues. He has also spoken about "a people-centric approach" and the spirit of "humanity first".

However, Singh says BRICS is simply not a priority for India and that in general, Delhi has not appreciated what many have interpreted as the "anti-western" turn the group has taken in recent times.

"With India as chair, India won't be comfortable with any kind of anti-western line," he says, pointing to the focus it places on defense ties with the US and trade ties with the west as a whole.

"India's idea of BRICS is more to look at improving trade ties, etc. In other words, can we do things which are beneficial to us without in any way being confrontational or critical of the West?"

Yet ironically, India's non-aligned status means it may actually be able to keep the bloc aligned.

"India adds clout because it has significant geopolitical weight and relationships across competing camps, making it an important bridge-builder," says Papa. "Its approach is likely to keep BRICS focused on practical cooperation and global governance reform rather than overt bloc politics."

What is BRICS for anyway?

BRICS is soon approaching its 18th birthday, so in a sense it should be coming of age. Yet the bloc has struggled for coherence in recent years amid doubt over its purpose.

The scale of what it could represent is not in doubt. It boasts nearly half the world's population among its members and around 40% of its GDP.

Last year, its joint declaration called for reforms of global governance, specifying representation on multilateral bodies such as the IMF and the World Bank. It also condemned tariffs and decried what it called the "polarization" of the international order.

"Ideologically, BRICS remains where it was during the last summit in Brazil, focused on practical, functional cooperation while seeking to avoid geopolitical tensions," says Papa.

She says that the expansion of the group from five to 11 members — if we include Saudi Arabia — has made it harder to reach consensus on various issues.

There are also now more autocracies among its members than democracies, while many members have tense bilateral relations. "These internal contradictions will always be hard to reconcile," says Singh.

What might happen this year

Nonetheless, Papa says she expects progress this year in three areas: trade, monetary cooperation, and agriculture. Discussions are likely to focus on improving trade between the members, alternative financial architecture for exchanging currencies and on issues around food security.

While talk of reforming global governance will still be central, she thinks BRICS' best hope to focus on the institutions which it agrees most on. For example, India is reluctant to press for UN reform but is keen for a co-ordinated approach from BRICS to trade and the WTO.

"India's WTO ambitions are shared by more members," she says, which makes movement in that area "more likely."

Yet many still share Singh's view that the group will "continue to underwhelm."

He says issues ranging from China's growing global dominance to the Trump administration's stance on tariffs have made the bloc's limited goals even harder to achieve.

"With the kind of world that we are in and the lack of coherence and internal contradictions that BRICS has, it's very unlikely that it will achieve anything major," he says.
